newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan economic reforms seen having mixed impact.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan economic reforms seen having mixed impact.

text.p: Pakistan's latest economic reform package is likely to boost inflation and depress growth, but should improve the trade and fiscal balance, ING Baring Securities said in a research report received on Monday.
"The impact of these fiscal measures is expected to be inflationary and recessionary in the short run," Kalim Aziz, head of research at ING Barings, said in the report.

He was analysing the likely impact of last week's economic stabilisation package, which included a 7.86 percent devaluation of the rupee against the dollar, an increase in the central bank's key repo rate to 20 percent from 17 and measures to narrow the budget deficit by 40 billion rupees ($995 million).
The budget-cutting steps included spending cuts, new taxes and a 10 percent increase in fuel prices.

Aziz said the package would drive annual inflation above the 8.5 percent target for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June). Consumer prices rose 10.8 percent in 1995/96, down from 13 percent the previous year, according to central bank figures.
Aziz said inflation would exceed 10 to 11 percent, but would not reflect the full extent of extra taxes or higher fuel prices because of renewed efforts to tighten the money supply.
Bankers say the rise in the repo rate will lift the overall interest rate structure, possibly restricting credit to the corporate sector and discouraging government borrowing.

Analysts say Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's government is unlikely to hit its economic growth target of 6.3 percent due to the tight money policy and cuts of about 20 billion rupees from development spending and seven billion rupees from current spending.
"A GDP growth target of 6.3 percent seems highly unlikely now. However, we should see GDP growth between 5.5 to 5.7 percent for the current fiscal year," Aziz said in the report.

He said the latest measures were harsh but necessary. "Pakistan's economy...has to rely on international investment. If measures are not taken to balance the books the likelihood of international investment falls drastically," Aziz said.
An International Monetary Fund mission arrived in Islamabad on Saturday to review the economy, a necessary prelude to any renewed disbursements of a stalled $600 million standby loan.
Aziz said all leading lending agencies were looking at the IMF's appraisal of Pakistan's economic performance.

He said it was unclear if the government, beset by political difficulties, would be able to fully implement the package, which is aimed at cutting the budget deficit to four percent of GDP from about 5.8 percent in 1995/96 and easing the trade gap.
"The devaluation addresses the trade deficit problem quite agressively and is likely to assist in boosting exports and curbing imports, thus, potentially leading to lower trade deficit," Aziz said.
The trade deficit swelled to $3.07 billion in 1995/96 from $2.26 billion in 1994/95. This year's target is $2.1 billion.
"We think a rational approach is to watch the IMF's response and then get into the market for investment with a six- to nine-month view by November," Aziz said in advice to investors.
